750.bp: When you search for images using text (or text using images), you're asking a computer to understand that the words 'fluffy white dog' and a photo of a poodle mean the same thing. This cross-modal retrieval matters everywhere: photo apps finding pictures by description, e-commerce matching product images to search queries, or accessibility systems describing images for visually impaired users.
750.wh: The difficulty is that visual and textual meaning don't map neatly. A photo of a dog has thousands of pixels with different colors and shapes, but the word 'dog' is just a sequence of letters. Most approaches flatten everything into one big number space (called an embedding space), but real images have sparse, localized details—like the specific texture of fur or a unique breed marker—that get drowned out when you're trying to match against many images at once.
750.ap: This paper builds a two-branch system: one path captures the whole-image meaning (global), the other zooms into specific regions (local). They also ask a language model to write extra descriptions of images, giving more semantic clues to work with. Then they train with a three-stage ranking process: first they make sure images of the same category cluster together, then they align matched images and text closely, finally they push apart unmatched pairs with a margin.
750.ww: Ranking in a shared space only works if the space itself respects the natural ordering of similarity. By adding written descriptions, you give the model more ways to see the same image—not just pixels but language. The multi-branch design captures both the forest (overall subject) and the trees (fine details), so neither gets lost. The three-stage training is like scaffolding: each step reinforces the previous one, so images end up properly sorted.
750.po: On four standard test sets, this method beats 12 competing approaches and improves retrieval accuracy by an average of 15.91%, meaning when you search 'dog' you get the right dog images in the top results far more often.

751.bp: Social media videos with comments are often sarcastic—someone might post 'Great job!' when they mean the opposite. Detecting the true sentiment (whether someone actually liked it or hated it) matters for brand monitoring, content moderation, and understanding public mood around breaking news, because sarcasm inverts the literal meaning.
751.wh: Sarcasm is deceptively hard because the words say one thing but the feeling is opposite. Most systems try to fuse (mix together) all available signals—the video, the audio tone, the text—into one blob of information to detect sarcasm. But when you mash positive and negative clues together, they cancel each other out into ambiguous mush, exactly when you need clarity most.
751.ap: Instead of mixing everything together, this method keeps text, video, and audio separate. For each type of media, it first extracts what sentiment it shows (positive, negative, or neutral) without fusing. Then it uses those separate sentiment judgments as a guide to understand the sarcasm feature, working on them independently instead of smashing them all together first.
751.ww: If you keep signals separate, you preserve their true polarities—positive stays positive, negative stays negative—so they can act as guides rather than drowning each other out. By conditioning the sarcasm interpretation on what each modality actually shows, the model can see the contradiction (words say yes, tone says no) instead of getting lost in a muddled mix.
751.po: The system better detects when social media comments are sarcastic versus genuine, which improves overall sentiment accuracy on videos where people commonly use sarcasm.

752.bp: Grouping similar things together (clustering) is everywhere: organizing products into categories, finding communities in social networks, or spotting disease subtypes in medical data. When your things are items connected by relationships—like authors linked by papers, or users joined by interests—clustering is trickier because the structure matters as much as the things themselves.
752.wh: The natural approach is to first learn a good vector representation of each item, then run k-means or similar to group them. But that two-step process ignores a key fact: the representation you learn might be perfect for one task (like prediction) but terrible for clustering. The model never gets direct feedback saying 'these should be together' or 'those should be apart' during representation learning.
752.ap: This method does representation learning and clustering simultaneously in one end-to-end system. It uses two learning goals working together: one learns good vector representations using ideas from similarity-based learning (comparing similar items), at both the single-item level and the group-of-connected-items level. The second goal refines those representations by actually clustering while learning, so the representations get shaped by clustering needs.
752.ww: If you optimize for clustering directly while learning representations, the vectors naturally arrange themselves into clusters—items that belong together get closer. By including both item-level and group-level similarity goals, the system respects both individual identity and structural connections, avoiding lonely outliers.
752.po: On eight datasets, this end-to-end approach beats methods that learn then cluster separately, because the representations are actually optimized for the clustering goal rather than something else.

753.bp: Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT learn from vast internet data, and sometimes they memorize things that shouldn't be there: private information, copyrighted text, or biased generalizations. 'Unlearning' means surgically removing that bad knowledge from an already-trained model, which is critical for privacy compliance and making systems trustworthy.
753.wh: Different pieces of unwanted knowledge are hard to forget at the same pace. Some facts are deeply entangled with other knowledge (forgetting 'X's address' also requires forgetting connections to 'X's work'), while others sit isolated and erase easily. If you push the same forgetting force equally on everything, some knowledge sticks around while other knowledge gets over-erased, leaving the model broken or obviously changed.
753.ap: This method treats unlearning like a game where the model and an opponent have conflicting goals. The opponent identifies which knowledge is hardest to forget (worst-case samples) and emphasizes those during training. The model then updates itself to forget exactly those hard samples. They offer two versions: one that groups hard samples and focuses on high-loss clusters, another that weights each sample smoothly based on how hard it is to forget.
753.ww: By focusing training effort on the hardest-to-forget knowledge, you ensure nothing slips through. Once the hard stuff is gone, the easier stuff naturally follows. The adaptive weighting approach spreads the 'forgetting pressure' smoothly rather than applying brute force, so the model doesn't get distorted trying to erase everything uniformly.
753.po: On benchmark datasets for unlearning, this approach erases unwanted knowledge more thoroughly than previous methods while keeping the model's other skills intact—it forgets better without breaking the system.

754.bp: Powerful AI foundation models now power search engines, recommendation systems, and content moderation on the web. But these models can be unfair (recommending only to majority groups), biased (learning stereotypes from data), opaque (no one knows why they chose something), or breakable under unusual real-world conditions, which erodes user trust and sometimes causes real harm.
754.wh: Foundation models are trained on messy, heterogeneous internet data that changes over time, at enormous scale where traditional safety checks fail. The sheer breadth of downstream uses means a single model flaw can ripple through dozens of applications. It's not clear how to even measure trustworthiness across fairness, transparency, causality, and robustness simultaneously.
754.ap: This workshop gathers researchers and practitioners to discuss how foundation models should be designed, tested, and deployed for trustworthiness. It emphasizes causal reasoning—understanding not just correlations ('clicks go up with this change') but cause-and-effect ('this change causes clicks to go up')—as a principled way to identify and fix unfairness and bias.
754.ww: Causal reasoning cuts through the noise: if you understand the causal mechanism by which a model produces output, you can spot where bias enters and surgically fix it. It also predicts what happens when you deploy a model in a new context, because you understand the underlying mechanisms rather than just historical patterns.
754.po: The workshop brings together tools and perspectives for making foundation models fairer, more transparent, and more robust—creating a roadmap for trustworthy AI on the web.

755.bp: Online ads compete for the tiny real estate on your screen—a search results page, a social media feed, or an app banner. An ad's success depends not just on where it sits but also on what other ads surround it. Crowding reduces effectiveness, too many ads cause banner blindness, and clutter online damages user experience and overall website value.
755.wh: Most auction systems for ad placement treat each slot independently: position A is worth some amount, position B is worth some other amount, and that's that. But in reality, an ad in position A is worth less when ads B and C right next to it are competing for the same user's attention. Standard auction theory breaks down because the value of an ad depends on context (nearby ads), not just position.
755.ap: This paper models screen positions as points in space, where an ad's value depends on its own bid plus a discount factor determined by nearby ads' bids. For some cases (when only the nearest neighbor matters), they design a fast algorithm that finds a good allocation and proves it can be implemented honestly (advertisers can't game it by lying). For 2D Euclidean layouts, they give a near-optimal solution.
755.ww: By explicitly modeling spatial interference, the mechanism respects the reality of how ads work. The discount factor captures crowding without requiring separate negotiations for each pair of ads. Proving the mechanism is 'truthful' (honest bidding is optimal) matters because advertisers will bid strategically—if they can't trick the system, it works fairly.
755.po: Platforms can now allocate ads to maximize both advertiser value and user experience by accounting for spatial interference, rather than treating slots as isolated islands.

756.bp: Scientists and data analysts often need to generate random versions of networks (social graphs, collaboration networks, food webs) or data tables while preserving certain properties—like 'keep the same number of connections per person' but shuffle who connects to whom. This helps test whether a pattern you see is real or just random chance.
756.wh: Creating randomized versions at scale is slow because existing methods scan the data multiple times and perform expensive calculations for each transformation. On large networks or matrices, even fast algorithms become bottlenecks, especially when you need thousands of random versions for statistical testing.
756.ap: This paper reformulates the randomization procedure as a sampling problem: instead of explicitly computing what vectors are valid, they use reservoir sampling (a standard technique for sampling from streams) and mathematical bounds to know when they've found good candidates without calculating everything. This lets them do the whole process in almost one pass over the data.
756.ww: Reframing as sampling avoids the need to compute and store all possibilities. Using upper bounds on what could be valid lets you skip expensive checks—if your bound says 'this is definitely valid', you don't need to verify. A single pass keeps data in fast memory and avoids redundant reads.
756.po: The speedup is 2x over prior methods, meaning researchers can generate random versions of large networks faster, speeding up hypothesis testing in network science.

757.bp: Tables on the web are everywhere: sports standings, financial reports, product specifications, weather forecasts. When someone asks 'What was the rainfall in Delhi last Tuesday?' they expect an AI to read the table layout, find the row for Delhi and the column for Tuesday, and extract the number. Web intelligence systems need to handle messy real-world tables, not toy examples.
757.wh: Tables are tricky because they mix layout (spatial structure) with meaning (what numbers represent what). A cell's meaning depends on which row and column it's in, sometimes across multiple levels of headers. Vision-language models (AI that reads images) can see the layout but sometimes miss the logical structure, especially when they need multi-step reasoning like 'sum all rainfall values in March' or 'find the row with the highest average'.
757.ap: This work creates a benchmark dataset that systematically varies two things independently: layout complexity (how tangled the table structure is, with merged cells or nested headers) and reasoning complexity (simple lookup versus arithmetic across rows, versus multi-hop logic). By splitting test cases along these dimensions, researchers can see where models actually struggle.
757.ww: You can't fix what you can't measure precisely. By separating layout challenges from reasoning challenges, you discover whether a model fails because it misreads the structure or because it can't follow the logic. This fine-grained view reveals which capabilities are actually weak.
757.po: Analysis shows state-of-the-art models still stumble on complex layouts and multi-step reasoning, pinpointing exactly where improvements are needed.

758.bp: Wireless coverage maps show signal strength at every location, crucial for network planning (where to put towers), interference management (avoiding overlaps), and smart resource allocation (directing traffic efficiently). Predicting these maps from sparse measurements and building geometry is a foundational problem in network engineering.
758.wh: Radio signals behave strangely: they have smooth variations over long distances (path loss from distance, shadowing from obstacles) but also rapid fine-grained fluctuations from bouncing signals arriving by multiple paths (multipath). A map prediction method needs to capture both smooth trends and fine details—too coarse and you miss coverage holes, too fine and noise drowns the signal.
758.ap: This paper treats map prediction as building from coarse to fine resolution, like painting a picture with brushes of increasing detail. They split the map into frequency bands (coarse signals, fine details) using Laplacian pyramids, then use a neural network to predict these bands progressively. The key innovation is using continuous numbers instead of discrete 'tokens' to avoid quantization artifacts.
758.ww: Multi-scale predictions naturally separate smooth variations (captured by coarse predictions) from details (captured by fine predictions). Using continuous values instead of rounding to discrete bins preserves subtle signal variations. Progressive refinement means each level can condition on coarser levels below, leveraging hierarchy.
758.po: On benchmark data, this method outperforms convolutional, transformer-based, generative, and diffusion baselines while staying fast enough for real-time deployment, balancing accuracy and speed.

759.bp: Recommender systems are supposed to discover new content, but they often get stuck promoting the same popular items (blockbuster movies, bestselling books, trending products) while less popular items get buried. This unfairness hurts content diversity, creator income, and user experience—people miss things they'd love because popularity drowns them out.
759.wh: Fixing popularity bias risks breaking recommendation accuracy: if you force exposure to unpopular items, users might get recommendations they hate, driving them away. It's also hard to see what's happening inside recommendation models (they're black boxes), so fixing bias often feels like flailing in the dark.
759.ap: This method trains a tool that mirrors the recommendation model's behavior but exposes which internal neurons encode 'this is a popular item' signals. By feeding the model synthetic users who love unpopular items and watching which neurons light up, the authors identify popularity-related neurons. They then tweak just those neurons to reduce popularity bias.
759.ww: If you can isolate the specific computations responsible for popularity bias, you can adjust them directly without breaking other parts of the model. Using synthetic test users lets you probe the model's behavior in controlled ways, revealing which neurons do what work.
759.po: On three public datasets, this approach significantly improves fairness (less popular items get more exposure) while keeping recommendation accuracy nearly unchanged—a concrete win for both algorithmic fairness and diversity.

760.bp: False information spreads faster online than corrections, especially when topics are polarized and communities reinforce each other's views. Early warning systems that can predict misinformation will emerge before it goes viral would let platforms intervene preemptively, reducing harm to public discourse and emergency response.
760.wh: Polarization and misinformation are linked but distinct: polarization means diverging opinions on a topic, misinformation means false claims. Existing systems predict misinformation after-the-fact (once it's already spread) by analyzing text content. Predicting it proactively requires identifying when a topic becomes fertile ground for misinformation—high polarization without verified facts.
760.ap: This work combines two pieces: first, an online clustering algorithm that watches a tweet stream and groups tweets by topic, detecting when topics suddenly explode in volume (bursts). Second, a sentiment classifier that understands how polarized the opinions are on each topic by measuring opinion divergence. These polarization metrics then feed into a machine learning model that predicts which topics will spawn misinformation.
760.ww: Tracking topics online as they emerge, rather than analyzing them afterward, gives early warning. Measuring sentiment divergence per topic (not overall) catches polarization specific to that topic, which is the actual signal. Adding polarization features to prediction models works because misinformation doesn't appear randomly—it emerges in polarized, unverified contexts.
760.po: On two COVID-19 tweet datasets, including polarization metrics improves misinformation prediction significantly and enables forecasting misinformation one month in advance, giving platforms time to act.

761.bp: News stories, reports, and social media posts describe events happening in specific places at specific times. Extracting that structured spatiotemporal information (who, where, when) lets systems track outbreaks, manage disasters, understand trends, and connect related events. But most information extraction pipelines are brittle and domain-specific.
761.wh: Traditional entity and event extraction requires manually coding rules or expensive labeled training data per domain. Building knowledge graphs requires engineers to pre-define all entity types and relationships. Generalization across domains is extremely hard because language use, event types, and entity categories vary wildly between, say, health data and news.
761.ap: This system leverages large language models (which know many domains) combined with spatial and temporal structure as 'anchors'. Users define what information they care about and how to organize it (e.g., 'give me disease cases by region and date'). The system uses large language models to extract and ground information, then stores it in a multidimensional warehouse organized by space and time. It includes quality checks and interactive visualization.
761.ww: Using space and time as universal dimensions avoids needing domain-specific ontologies—any domain has space and time. Large language models bring cross-domain knowledge and flexibility. Interactive validation lets users correct errors on-the-fly, continuously improving quality.
761.po: On a public health dataset, this system extracts spatiotemporal entities more accurately than using language models alone, and the live dashboard supports discovery of patterns (where did cases spike, when did trends shift).

762.bp: Designing new drugs or polymers means finding molecules with desired properties (strong, safe, biodegradable). Generative models can propose candidate molecules, and recent advances use diffusion processes that start with noise and gradually 'refine' toward realistic structures. But when you want to control multiple properties at once (make it strong AND biocompatible AND cheap), existing methods struggle to honor all constraints.
762.wh: Most generative approaches directly sample from the desired distribution, but they often simplify: treating multiple conditions as independent or averaging them together, which violates the joint distribution (the true relationship between all conditions). This causes models to generate molecules that are good on average but poor on each individual constraint.
762.ap: This method models molecule generation as a sequence of refinement steps, like sculpting: you start with a rough shape and gradually detail it. Each step adjusts the molecular structure to move toward configurations that satisfy multiple conditions together (jointly). To train this, they use a two-stage approximation: first they train on early steps, then later steps, avoiding the computational cost of training every step equally.
762.ww: Markov chains (step-by-step processes where the future depends only on the current state) naturally handle joint distributions—at each step, all conditions influence the next step. Gradual refinement gives the model more opportunities to satisfy constraints than one-shot generation.
762.po: On polymer and small molecule datasets, this approach generates molecules with better control over multiple properties compared to traditional methods, improving both property match and structural validity.

763.bp: Large language models respond to instructions (prompts), and how you phrase an instruction massively changes the response. A tiny wording change can mean the difference between 'correct answer' and 'nonsense'. Since prompts are now how millions of people use AI, sharing practices and understanding what works is a growing need.
763.wh: Prompt effectiveness is unpredictable and brittle. There's no clear theory of why one phrasing works and another doesn't. People resort to trial-and-error, failing to find good prompts. As models scale up and are deployed in critical roles, this ad-hoc 'fail and retry' approach isn't good enough.
763.ap: This workshop brings together academics and industry practitioners to discuss prompt engineering: how to design instructions that reliably work, new strategies for prompting, guardrails to make prompts safer, and emerging paradigms for using language models beyond simple instruction-following.
763.ww: Collective experience and structured exchange help practitioners build intuitions and share patterns. By gathering people from different domains (some working on science, others on creative writing, others on code generation), the workshop identifies cross-cutting principles.
763.po: Attendees leave with better practices for prompting, curated optimization strategies, and real-world results demonstrating what works.

764.bp: AI research agents that search papers, run experiments, and synthesize findings could accelerate scientific discovery. But how do you evaluate whether an agent actually did good research? A single score like 'Pass@1' (did it answer correctly?) misses what matters: Was the reasoning sound? Did it waste compute? Is it actually robust or did it get lucky?
764.wh: Conventional evaluation metrics focus only on whether the final answer matches ground truth. But an agent could stumble on the right answer by accident, or follow a wasteful reasoning path, or be brittle (fail on slight input variations). These flaws don't show up in outcome-based scores, creating a 'high-score illusion' where metrics look good but the agent is unreliable.
764.ap: This framework evaluates the entire reasoning trajectory, not just the endpoint. It computes a score combining accuracy, efficiency (how many steps?), and cognitive quality (how well-grounded in evidence?). Separately, they measure 'latent capability' by determining how much hints/scaffolding an agent needs to solve problems, revealing whether it's genuinely capable or just pattern-matching.
764.ww: Process matters because a fragile agent might fail on similar problems despite getting one right. By scoring efficiency and evidence grounding, you catch wasteful reasoning. Measuring how much help is needed reveals true capability—an agent that needs hand-holding is not as capable as one that figures it out independently.
764.po: This framework provides fine-grained rankings revealing trade-offs (accuracy vs. efficiency) and latent capabilities entirely hidden by singular metrics, guiding research toward actually robust agents.
